quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on the vocabulary of pointed, herringbone, broken and curved twills.

questions.q: What does a pointed (waved) twill do to the ordinary twill?
options: Shifts every second pick by two picks
Reverses the draft so the diagonal meets itself point to point
Re-orders the picks so the line never runs more than two ends
Changes the step gradually so the line bends
questions.explain: A pointed twill turns the draft back on itself, so the twill line runs one way, then the other, meeting at a point. The shifted join is the herringbone and the re-ordered picks the broken twill.

questions.q: How does a herringbone differ from a pointed twill?
options: It uses a steeper twill angle
It reverses the line but keeps the join unbroken
It reverses the line and cuts the join by shifting the second half two picks
questions.explain: In a herringbone the second half runs the other way and is shifted (cut) by two picks, so the twill lines do not meet point to point; that break gives the fish-bone look. A pointed twill leaves the join unbroken.

questions.q: A twill whose line is interrupted every few ends, giving the crow's foot effect, is called a
questions.explain: The lecture defines the broken twill as one that interrupts the line every few ends and names the 2/2 version crow's foot.

questions.q: What is changed to make a curved twill?
options: The step, which changes gradually, e.g. 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 ends per pick
The direction of the draft at every fourth end
questions.explain: A curved twill changes the step gradually so the twill line bends. The healds stay the same because only the lifting order changes.

questions.q: In a cut herringbone, warp floats meet weft floats at the join.
questions.explain: Because the second half is both reversed and inverted, a warp float on one side of the cut faces a weft float on the other; that is the sharp line that makes the fish-bone.

questions.q: Which derivative gives the typical fish-bone appearance?
questions.explain: The cut join of the herringbone produces the fish-bone (herring bone) stripe. A broken twill has a small all-over crow's-foot effect instead.

questions.q: Another name for the pointed twill is
questions.explain: The lecture uses waved and pointed interchangeably. Crow's foot is the broken 2/2 twill and a cut twill is a herringbone.

questions.q: A broken twill has a longer continuous diagonal than the regular twill it comes from.
questions.explain: The opposite: in the crow's foot the picks are re-ordered so the diagonal never runs more than two ends, which is shorter than in the unbroken twill.

questions.q: In twill terminology the step means
options: The number of healds in the draft
The number of ends by which the lift moves on each successive pick
The number of picks in one repeat
The length of the longest float
questions.explain: The step is how far the lifting pattern advances on each pick; a step of 1 gives the ordinary 45° line and a changing step gives the curved twill.

questions.q: Which derivative keeps the peg plan of a plain 2/2 twill and changes only the draft?
questions.explain: A pointed twill reverses the draft while the lifting plan stays an ordinary 2/2 twill. Broken and curved twills alter the lifting order instead.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Repeat sizes, heald counts, pick orders and what the step does to the angle of the twill line.

questions.q: What is the repeat of the lecture's waved (pointed) 2/2 twill?
questions.explain: The pointed draft 1 2 3 4 3 2 uses six ends before it repeats, while the lifting plan is still the four-pick 2/2 twill: 6 ends × 4 picks.

questions.q: What is the repeat of the lecture's cut herringbone 2/2?
questions.explain: Four ends run one way and four the other, so eight ends across; the lifting still repeats on four picks.

questions.q: The broken 2/2 twill (crow's foot) repeats on
questions.explain: The four picks of a 2/2 twill are simply re-ordered, so the repeat stays 4 ends × 4 picks.

questions.q: In which order are the picks of a 2/2 twill woven to produce the crow's foot?
questions.explain: The lecture gives the order 1, 3, 2, 4. The straight order 1, 2, 3, 4 is the ordinary twill and 4, 3, 2, 1 only reverses its direction.

questions.q: On a square sett, if the step rises from one end per pick to two ends per pick, what happens to the twill line?
options: It becomes flatter (a lower angle to the weft)
questions.explain: With a step of 2 the line advances two ends for every pick, so it leans over and becomes flatter. That gradual change of angle is what makes the curved twill bend.

questions.q: The pointed draft for a four-heald twill is written
questions.explain: The draft climbs to heald 4 and turns back without repeating the turning healds: 1 2 3 4 3 2. Repeating 4 and 1 at the turns would give a different, eight-end draft.

questions.q: How many healds does the 8-end cut herringbone 2/2 need?
questions.explain: Ends 5–8 are the inverse of a reversed 2/2 twill; their movements are the same four movements as ends 1–4, just in a different order, so four healds carry all eight ends.

questions.q: A curved twill needs more healds than the straight twill it comes from.
questions.explain: Only the lifting order changes in a curved twill; the ends are still drafted straight, so the heald count is unchanged.

questions.q: In a waved twill the reversal that produces the zigzag is made in the
options: Draft (the order of ends on the healds)
questions.explain: The lecture says the pointed twill reverses the draft; the peg plan stays an ordinary twill.

questions.q: The herringbone in the lecture shifts the second half by two picks.
questions.explain: The join is broken by shifting the second half two picks, so the diagonals do not meet; the lecture describes this as the cut.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting ends, healds, floats and filled squares on the point paper of each twill derivative.

questions.q: A pointed draft on a 4-heald twill runs 1 2 3 4 3 2. How many ends are in one repeat of the draft?
questions.explain: Up 1 2 3 4 and back 3 2: 2 × 4 − 2 = 6 ends, because the two turning healds are not repeated.

questions.q: If the same pointed draft is made on an 8-heald twill (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 7 6 5 4 3 2), how many ends does one repeat contain?
questions.explain: 2 × 8 − 2 = 14 ends, since healds 8 and 1 occur only once in the repeat.

questions.q: A herringbone 2/2 repeats on 8 ends. How many complete repeats are there in a stripe of 96 ends?
questions.explain: 96 ÷ 8 = 12 repeats of the herringbone across the stripe.

questions.q: In the crow's foot (broken 2/2 twill) the lecture says the diagonal never runs more than how many ends?
questions.explain: Re-ordering the picks 1, 3, 2, 4 limits any diagonal run to two ends.

questions.q: The lecture's curved twill advances one end per pick for 5 picks, then two ends per pick for 5 picks. By how many ends has the lifting advanced after the 10 picks?
questions.explain: 5 × 1 + 5 × 2 = 15 ends of advance in 10 picks. On a 5-end 3/2 base, 15 is three whole repeats, so the design closes after 10 picks.

questions.q: How many healds does the pointed 2/2 twill drafted 1 2 3 4 3 2 require?
questions.explain: The highest heald number in the draft is 4, and ends 5 and 6 return to healds 3 and 2, so four healds carry all six ends.

questions.q: The herringbone 2/2 is drawn on 8 ends × 4 picks. How many squares are filled (end up)?
questions.explain: In a 2/2 weave every end is up for half the picks, so half of 8 × 4 = 32 squares are filled: 16.

questions.q: The waved 2/2 twill is drawn on 6 ends × 4 picks. How many squares are filled?
questions.explain: Each of the 6 ends is lifted on 2 of the 4 picks: 6 × 2 = 12 filled squares.

questions.q: With the crow's foot pick order 1, 3, 2, 4, which original pick of the 2/2 twill is woven third?
questions.explain: Reading the order 1, 3, 2, 4, the third pick woven is original pick 2.

questions.q: In the 3/1 herringbone drawn on 8 ends × 4 picks, how many ends are lifted on any one pick in the warp-faced half of 4 ends?
questions.explain: A 3/1 twill lifts three ends out of every four on each pick, so three of the four ends in that half are up on any pick.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Choosing the right twill derivative for a customer and knowing what changes on the loom — draft, peg plan or both.

questions.q: A suiting buyer asks for the classic fish-bone stripe. Which weave should the mill offer?
questions.explain: Herringbone's cut join gives the fish-bone look. A pointed twill gives a zigzag with the lines meeting, and a broken twill a small crow's-foot texture.

questions.q: A designer wants a zigzag whose diagonals meet point to point on an existing four-heald 2/2 twill loom. What should change?
options: Change the draft to a pointed draft and keep the peg plan
questions.explain: A pointed twill is made by reversing the draft; the lifting plan stays the same 2/2 twill and no extra healds are needed.

questions.q: The customer likes the reversed diagonal but not the twill lines meeting at the points. What should the designer do?
options: Cut the join by shifting the second half two picks (herringbone)
questions.explain: Shifting the second half breaks the join so the lines no longer meet — that is exactly the herringbone. Changing the step would give a curved twill, not a cut join.

questions.q: A mill needs a small, non-directional all-over effect from a 2/2 twill using the same four healds and straight draft. Which derivative fits?
questions.explain: The crow's foot only re-orders the picks, so the straight draft and four healds stay; its diagonal never exceeds two ends, so there is no dominant direction.

questions.q: A curved twill can be woven with the same healds and straight draft as its base twill, because only the lifting order changes.
questions.explain: The curved twill advances the lifting by a changing number of ends per pick; that lives in the peg plan, so the draft and heald count are untouched.

questions.q: When preparing the dobby pegging for a crow's foot from a 2/2 twill, the weaver should peg the picks in which order?
questions.explain: The lecture's broken 2/2 twill is obtained by re-ordering the picks 1, 3, 2, 4. The straight order would weave an ordinary twill.

questions.q: Which derivative is produced by changing the peg plan rather than the draft?
options: Herringbone made by reversing the draft
questions.explain: The broken twill re-orders the picks, i.e. the lifting plan. Pointed twills and draft-reversed herringbones change the threading.

questions.q: A sample shows the diagonal running one way for a few ends, then the other way, with the lines meeting cleanly at each turn. What is it?
questions.explain: Lines that meet point to point at each reversal identify the pointed twill; in a herringbone the join is cut and the lines are offset.

questions.q: A weaver reverses the second half of a herringbone but forgets to shift it. What results?
options: A pointed twill, because the lines now meet at the join
questions.explain: Without the two-pick shift the join is unbroken and the diagonals meet point to point, which is the pointed twill, not the herringbone the customer wanted.

questions.q: A loom is pegged for the lecture's curved 3/2 twill. In the second five picks the twill line is seen to
options: Become flatter because the lift now advances two ends per pick
Become steeper because the lift advances two ends per pick
questions.explain: Advancing two ends per pick lays the line over at a lower angle to the weft, so the line bends and flattens; it does not reverse.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning about drafts, joins and heald counts, and the errors students make most often.

questions.q: Ends 5–8 of the lecture's cut herringbone 2/2 are the inverse of a reversed 2/2 twill. Which draft on four healds weaves the eight ends?
questions.explain: Reversing gives heald order 4 3 2 1; inverting swaps each end's lifts for its sinks, which in a 2/2 twill moves it two picks along, so heald 4 becomes 2, 3 becomes 1, 2 becomes 4 and 1 becomes 3: 1 2 3 4 2 1 4 3.

questions.q: A pointed draft for a 2/2 twill repeats on 6 ends. How many repeats of the draft are there in a warp of 120 ends?
questions.explain: 120 ÷ 6 = 20 repeats of the pointed draft.

questions.q: A student claims the pointed twill of 6 ends × 4 picks needs six healds. What is wrong?
options: Ends 5 and 6 repeat the movements of ends 3 and 2, so four healds suffice
Only two healds are needed because it is a 2/2 weave
Eight healds are needed, one per pick
questions.explain: Healds equal the number of different end movements, not the number of ends. The draft 1 2 3 4 3 2 returns to healds 3 and 2, so four healds are enough.

questions.q: In the crow's foot the twill diagonal never runs more than two ends.
questions.explain: That is the lecture's description of the broken 2/2 twill with picks ordered 1, 3, 2, 4.

questions.q: A curved twill advances 1 end per pick for 5 picks, 2 ends per pick for the next 5 and 3 ends per pick for the last 5. By how many ends has the lift advanced over the 15 picks?
questions.explain: 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 ends of advance; on a 5-end base that is six whole repeats, so the design closes.

questions.q: Which derivative combines a reversal of direction with an inversion (warp floats become weft floats) in its second half?
questions.explain: The herringbone's second half runs the other way and is inverted, which is why warp floats meet weft floats at the join. A pointed twill reverses without inverting.

questions.q: Which statement about the pointed twill is FALSE?
options: Its lifting plan is an ordinary twill
Its draft turns back on itself
Its diagonals meet point to point
Its join is shifted by two picks
questions.explain: The two-pick shift belongs to the herringbone. In a pointed twill the join is unbroken and the lines meet point to point.

questions.q: A broken twill is produced by re-ordering the picks, so the draft stays straight.
questions.explain: Only the peg plan changes; the ends remain on a straight draft of four healds.

questions.q: In the lecture's waved twill drafted 1 2 3 4 3 2, which end repeats the movement of end 2?
questions.explain: End 6 is on heald 2, so it lifts exactly as end 2 does. End 5 is on heald 3, repeating end 3.

questions.q: A herringbone 2/2 is drawn 8 ends wide. How many squares are filled on each pick, and why?
options: 4, because every 2/2 pick lifts half the ends in each half
2, because only the first half lifts
6, because the second half is inverted
questions.explain: In both halves each pick lifts two of four ends, so 2 + 2 = 4 of the 8 ends are up on every pick. Inversion changes which ends are up, not how many.
